description:
Hi! We’re Grass on Mars, a team from Dushanbe, Tajikistan passionate about space exploration and the future of humanity on the Red Planet.

We believe Mars is humanity’s next frontier. We want to explore how people could one day live, work and thrive there, using real NASA data and creative thinking. Our name says it all: one day, even grass could grow on Mars.
summary:
Picture this: you're one of the first humans on Mars. No rescue team, no second chances. Pick the wrong spot or the wrong path and the mission is over. The data that could save you exists, but it's scattered across dozens of NASA missions and impossible to read in the middle of a red desert.

So we built Marswalk. It packs 13 NASA datasets (HiRISE and MOLA elevation, CTX imagery, geologic maps, ice, radiation and real rover weather) into one map and a 3D globe you can spin. First, you compare 14 places where a crew could work: where's the water, where's the science, where's it safe? Then you drop into Jezero Crater, tap a target and get four routes: fastest, safest, shortest and a science detour past real Perseverance sites. Every route shows distance, slopes, time and suit oxygen, and ends with a clear GO or NO GO. You can even swap your boots for one of three NASA rover concepts and watch the route change.

And you're never alone: Zyro, our friendly alien sidekick, helps with everything. He explains every call in plain words and shows the data behind it.

Our numbers are real: our air pressure estimate is within 3% of what Perseverance actually measured.
details:
Why we built Marswalk

Imagine standing on Mars for the first time. Help is months away, your suit holds about eight hours of oxygen, and the ground ahead hides steep slopes, loose rock and the risk of a dust storm. NASA has already mapped Mars in remarkable detail, but that knowledge is spread across dozens of instruments, missions and archives. In that moment, an astronaut needs just three answers: Where should we work? How do we get there? Will we make it back?

Marswalk gives those answers. We are Grass on Mars, a team of four from Dushanbe, Tajikistan, and we built a tool that turns NASA science into decisions a crew can trust.

What it does

Marswalk guides a crew from choosing a region on the planet to taking a safe step on real terrain, in three steps.

1. Compare territories. On a 2D map or a 3D globe, the crew compares 14 candidate sites. A suitability index combines five parameters (water and ice, science value, safety, sunlight and radiation), and users can change the weights to fit their mission. Sites outside NASA exploration-zone limits are removed before ranking. A robustness test runs 1,000 random trials, varying every weight by up to ±50% and adding measurement uncertainty, to check that the result does not depend on our assumptions. The answer is honest: Arcadia Planitia wins for a long-term base because ice lies about a metre below the surface, and Jezero Crater wins for astrobiology and is walkable from the landing site.

2. Plan the walk. In Jezero, the crew picks a science target and Marswalk computes routes on real terrain with an A* search. Three strategies can be compared side by side: Shortest, Lowest terrain risk and Science priority. Terrain risk weighs slope (40%), roughness and drops (25%), obstacles (15%) and data uncertainty (20%). Every route shows distance, elevation profile, hazards, walking time and oxygen use, then gets a clear GO or NO GO against real mission rules: an 8-hour suit, a 30% oxygen reserve, slopes under 15° and a return before 17:30 local time. A dust slider shows how a storm changes the plan.

3. Walk with Zyro. Zyro, our friendly alien mission assistant, walks with the crew every step of the way. He explains each recommendation with the data behind it, answers questions, tells the mission story aloud, and with one click rewrites any calculation in simple words.

The science underneath

Marswalk uses 14 sources, 13 of them from NASA, collected by five missions: Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Curiosity and Perseverance. These include MOLA and CTX elevation, HiRISE and CTX images, THEMIS infrared, CRISM minerals, SHARAD radar, MEDA weather, RAD radiation, MOXIE oxygen results and Perseverance waypoints. Eight transparent formulas turn the data into decisions: barometric pressure, sunlight by latitude, Tobler walking speed adjusted for a suit, oxygen reserve, radiation dose and the weighted site index, among others.

We check our models against reality. At Jezero, our pressure model gives 774 Pa, while Perseverance’s MEDA station measured 754–771 Pa on sol 100: a difference of less than 3%. All results can be downloaded as CSV, JSON and GeoJSON, so anyone can verify them.

Mission concept: Grass on Mars I

Marswalk is the operations tool of a full mission plan. Four astronauts live about 500 sols at Jezero. Cargo lands one launch window early, so the habitat, power and oxygen plant are working before the crew arrives. Water comes from about 98% life-support recycling and from hydrated minerals. The plan includes science goals mapped to NASA’s MEPAG goals, budgets for radiation, oxygen and power, and six key risks with mitigations. Minimum success means 10 Marswalks to 4 targets, 20 documented samples and the first seeds germinating. Full success means 40+ Marswalks, 60+ samples, oxygen made on Mars and a harvest grown with Martian water. That is the dream behind our name: one day, grass on Mars.

Benefits

- Safety before every step: oxygen, slope, dust and daylight are checked before anyone leaves the habitat.

- Explainable, not a black box: every number links to a NASA dataset and a formula you can check.

- More science per walk: routes can pass real Perseverance science targets, so every hour in a suit counts.

- Easy to use: it runs in a browser, and Zyro explains everything in plain language.

Impact on Earth and in Tajikistan

Tajikistan is a mountain country, and the same engine can keep people safe here. Replace Mars elevation with NASA’s free global elevation data, and the slope, daylight and supply checks help mountain rescue teams, geology field trips and trekkers. The Pamirs are a natural Mars analog: a cold, dry plateau around 4,000 m where the air is about 62 kPa, compared with 92 kPa in Dushanbe and only 0.77 kPa at Jezero. Our glaciers, including the 77 km Fedchenko Glacier, feed the Amu Darya, and the same orbital imaging and radar ideas used to find ice on Mars help track glaciers from space. Marswalk is also a learning tool: students can explore real NASA data and check every number themselves.

What makes it creative

Most Mars maps show the planet. Marswalk helps a person act on it. It connects the whole chain, from comparing regions across a planet to planning one safe walk on real terrain, and it makes complex science friendly through a character people actually want to listen to.

Tools we used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web app; Leaflet for 2D maps; three.js for the 3D globe and terrain; Python to prepare elevation data; a server-side A* route planner; NASA Mars Trek, PDS archives and USGS Astrogeology for data; Claude as the AI behind Zyro’s answers and voice.

What we considered, and our limits

We designed for real mission rules, not ideal conditions: suit endurance, oxygen reserve, steep ground, dust, daylight and radiation. We are also open about our limits. Routes and hazard scores are planning estimates, not certified safety thresholds. The terrain model is 20 m, so features smaller than about 60 m are not resolved. Weather comes from archived sols, not forecasts. Outside Jezero, terrain is coarser (463 m), and the landing check does not yet see rock abundance or soil strength. The 18 m footprint of a rock does not fit in a 60 m cell, and we would rather say so than hide it. Showing what we don’t know is part of building a tool astronauts can trust.
